extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of logic, philosophy, rhetoric, and critical thinking (educated readers learning to detect fallacies and evaluate arguments)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for detecting and classifying common fallacies in inductive and deductive reasoning, with examples and warnings about ambiguous language, bad classification, false analogies, and syllogistic errors. Intended to teach critical evaluation of arguments and to prevent misapplication of premises.

rubrics_metrics.name: False Analogy
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments that infer from similarity in some respects to similarity in others where the essential point differs (e.g., inferring disease from increase in size because of an analogy between metropolis and heart).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require that 'the same law is really operating' in both cases; show that between the known resemblance and the inferred one there is a causal connection. Examples given: Pythagorean numerological inferences, assuming social/metaphorical resemblances prove the same causal relations. Beware analogies drawn from superficial resemblances or from attributes that are irrelevant to the disputed question.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metaphor is not proof (metaphors as assertions of a proof)
rubrics_metrics.description: A metaphor or analogy does not itself prove a proposition; 'a metaphor, then, is not to be considered as an argument, but as an assertion that an argument exists.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use metaphors to aid apprehension and to suggest possible grounds of the conclusion, but do not accept them as evidence. An apt metaphor can have logical value only insofar as it points to an actual causal parity or to a previously known case where those grounds sufficed (examples: D’Alembert's eagle-and-serpent metaphor can suggest mechanisms). However, metaphors may mislead when the similarity is only verbal (Bacon's river-froth illustration: levity ≠ buoyancy). Always ask: what is the real structural/causal resemblance the metaphor relies on?

rubrics_metrics.name: Bad classification (source of fallacies of generalization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bringing together under one name things that have no common properties, or only trivial ones, so that general propositions about the class are invalid (e.g., extending the notion 'Humidum' to many heterogeneous phenomena).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid forming classes by slight or temerarious abstraction from ordinary cases. Verify that the supposed common property is substantial and constant across the class. Examples: misuse of broad ancient categories (κίνησις, Generation/Corruption) shows how heterogeneous concepts produce abortive theorizing. Check definitions and whether the predicate applies uniformly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Erroneous conversion of propositions (simple conversion fallacy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mistakenly inferring the converse: e.g., from 'All A are B' concluding 'All B are A', or treating 'If A then B' as 'If B then A'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply syllogistic/formal checks: the proper simple conversion of universal affirmatives is not generally allowable. For hypotheticals, remember the correct converse is: if the consequent is false, the antecedent is false (contrapositive reasoning), but 'If the consequent is true, the antecedent is true' is invalid. Expose this by formalizing the propositions where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mistaking the truth of a conclusion for truth of premises (reverse of reductio / illicit inference from desirable conclusions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Accepting a doctrine because it leads to true or desirable conclusions, and treating those conclusions as proof of the premises (confusing consequence with antecedent truth).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish evidential direction: true consequences do not establish the truth of premises unless the link is shown bidirectional. Beware systems adopted because their consequences support other cherished beliefs; check premises by independent induction or evidence, not by the attractiveness of results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confusion of contrary and contradictory propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Failing to distinguish that 'contrary' propositions can both be false while 'contradictory' propositions cannot; leading to the practical error of treating the reverse of a wrong as right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When testing a claim, force it into explicit propositions and check whether supposed opposites are contraries or contradictories. Making the error expressible in explicit logical form is an effective method to expose it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vicious syllogisms (undistributed middle / illicit process / more than three terms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Syllogistic fallacies arising from having more than three terms, an undistributed middle term, or illicitly distributing a term (one of the classic defective syllogism forms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set out the premises formally to reveal hidden terms and distribution. The rules of the syllogism protect against these errors: if premises are fully stated, many fallacies vanish. Beware suppressed premises introduced to patch the syllogism; demand explicitness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changing premises in a chain of argument (à dicto secundum quid ad dictum simpliciter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Slipping from an asserted proposition qualified in the premises into an unqualified form in the later argument, i.e., using a truth 'secundum quid' as if true 'simpliciter'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track qualifications and conditions attached to earlier propositions and preserve them when those propositions are used as premises later. Examples: Mercantile Theory (treating 'whatever brings in money enriches' without its provisos), tithe/rent reasoning, Wakefield colonization objection. Check that the context and necessary conditions (time, accompanying circumstances) have not been dropped.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dropping temporal or other implicit conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Using propositions that are true only under a time-condition or other limiting circumstance as if they hold at all times (e.g., interpreting 'prices, profits, wages... always find their level' as meaning they are always at that level).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify implicit conditions (especially of time) required for a premise to be true. When a general principle is cited, ask: 'under what circumstances or time-frame is this asserted?' Failure to preserve such conditions leads to wrong inferences about present or differing situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misapplication of abstract truths (reasoning from 'true in the abstract' as absolute)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying principles that are true only 'in the abstract' (i.e., with all modifying causes absent) to real-world cases where modifying causes exist, producing invalid conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize when a principle is an idealization; explicitly list modifying causes that are suppressed by the abstract claim. This misapplication is common and especially dangerous in political and social reasoning—avoid treating abstract maxims as unqualified laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity of terms (Fallacies of Confusion / ambiguous middle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments founded on ambiguity when a term is used in one sense in the premises and another in the conclusion, or when the middle term has multiple senses (including paronymous/conjugate words).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure consistent meanings across premises and conclusion; when words have several senses, disambiguate before inferring. Examples and pitfalls: paronymous words (project/projector, presumption/presume), etymological fallacies (assuming original meaning controls current usage, e.g., 'representative'), and many practical ambiguities ('money' as currency vs capital; 'influence of property'; 'theory' proper vs vulgar sense; 'church' meaning clergy vs whole body). Formalize terms and test whether a shift in sense sneaks into the argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacy from etymology (using etymological meaning to settle current sense)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assuming that the original or etymological sense of a word dictates its current legitimate meaning in argument (example: treating 'representative' as bound to its root 'represent').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect law, custom, and established usage as determinants of meaning in practice; do not let etymology override the sense fixed by context or convention. When someone appeals to etymology to discredit a legitimate 'theory' or role, require demonstration that the etymological sense is relevant to the claim being made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity in pronouns and implicit agents
rubrics_metrics.description: Confusion arising from ambiguous pronouns or implicit references (e.g., Descartes's 'I' meaning will vs laws of my nature), leading to illicit inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make implicit references explicit: rewrite arguments replacing pronouns with the intended referents and test whether the steps remain valid. If meaning shifts (will vs nature, collective vs individual), the inference may fail even if superficially plausible.
